posts.content:
What is #AI? I've recently started defining AI as "a bundle of capabilities for interacting with digital information" - #AIaaBC (AI as a Bundle of Capabilities) if you will. AI can take in digital information in a variety of forms - a string of words, an image, a file. AI can produce information in a number of digital formats - a string of words, an image, a video. AI can also organize, decide, and execute - when the instructions and activities all live in 0s and 1s. It's not a magical black box; it is a collaborator that can take in, act on, and kick out digital information.

Here is a one shot infographic from M365 Copilot presenting AIaaBC. 

Prompt: "Use the labels and emojis as they show up in this AIaaBC model. Make it pop..."

Then I simply pasted in the list of AIaaBC capability families (sense, produce, organize, decide, execute) and the specific capabilities in each family (such as "interpret language" and "recognize speech" in the "sense" family) with their definitions and emojis. 

More to come on both AIaaBC (I think it has legs, and have already started using it to describe AI evolution) and on my continued journey of leaning in to #M365Copilot.

Once we understand it's capabilities, we can align them to our tasks, challenges, and aspirations. That's how we unlock AI integration.

author.headline: Agentic AI: The Next Evolution of Intelligence

posts.content:
Agentic AI: The Next Evolution of Intelligence

We’re entering a new era of AI. Beyond chatbots and predictive models, Agentic AI is here systems that can:

- Take goals from humans
- Plan & act independently
- Adapt to change
- Seek help only when necessary

Unlike traditional AI, Agentic AI is autonomous, goal-driven, and context-aware making it a true collaboratorinstead of just a tool.

6 Core Traits of Agentic AI:
- Autonomy
- Goal Orientation
- Planning
- Reasoning
- Adaptability
- Context Awareness

5 Core Components that bring this to life:
- Brain (LLM)
- Orchestrator (LangGraph style)
- Tools
- Memory
- Supervisor

Imagine AI that doesn’t just assist but takes ownership of goals and delivers outcomes. That’s the future being built today.

I’ve broken this down in detail (with visuals) in my latest blog here: 
https://lnkd.in/eYs-uBgX

Question for you:
Do you see Agentic AI as the next big leap in enterprise AI adoption, or are we still years away from trusting autonomous AI systems?

Building AI Agents from Scratch!
AI agents aren’t a thing of the future anymore—they’re here, shaping industries today. From analyzing medical scans to drafting legal summaries, they’re proving just how powerful specialized AI can be.

Dixit Tiwari framework lays out 9 practical steps to get started:
 1️⃣ Define your agent’s role & goal
 2️⃣ Map structured inputs & outputs
 3️⃣ Prompt & fine-tune its behavior
 4️⃣ Add reasoning & tool usage
 5️⃣ Build multi-agent logic (if needed)
 6️⃣ Integrate memory & long-term context (RAG)
 7️⃣ Enable voice/vision (optional)
 8️⃣ Format the output (human or machine-ready)
 9️⃣ Wrap it in a UI or API (optional)
💡 Takeaway: Building effective AI agents goes beyond plugging into GPT. Success comes from orchestrating inputs, outputs, reasoning, and memory so your agent can operate reliably in real-world workflows.

Tools to explore: LangChain, Pydantic AI, OpenAI, Claude, CrewAI, ChromaDB, FAISS, ElevenLabs, and more.

Pro tip: Start small. Choose one use case, define the agent’s role, structure its inputs/outputs—and you’ll be surprised how quickly your first AI agent comes to life!

#AI #ArtificialIntelligence #Agents #LangChain #OpenAI #MachineLearning #Innovation

🚀 Agentic AI — The Next Frontier of AI Systems

We’re moving from static AI models to dynamic agentic systems — where AI doesn’t just respond, but acts, plans, and collaborates.

Here are the 4 foundational design patterns shaping this new wave 👇

1️⃣ Reflection
Agents that learn from their own mistakes — evaluating their outputs, reasoning about errors, and improving iteratively.
(Think of it as “AI debugging itself.”)

2️⃣ Tool Use
Instead of being limited to trained knowledge, agents now invoke APIs, browse data, or run code to accomplish real tasks.
(Bridging reasoning with real-world action.)

3️⃣ Planning
From single-turn responses to multi-step reasoning chains, agents now plan ahead — setting subgoals, executing them sequentially, and adapting dynamically.

4️⃣ Multi-Agent Collaboration
The next leap: networks of specialized agents that communicate, negotiate, and coordinate to solve complex problems collectively.

🔹 Together, these patterns move AI from prompt → response to goal → outcome.

We’re not just teaching AI to think — we’re teaching it to act intelligently.

author.name: Nofil Khan
author.headline: What’s the difference between an AI agent and AI workflow?

posts.content:
What’s the difference between an AI agent and AI workflow? The main difference is that in an Agent, the AI has the choice to determine how many LLM calls to make, what tools to use and when to stop its own loop. Agents are used in situations where the solution isn’t clear. A workflow is for when you already know what the output is supposed to be. You can create pre determined steps to get there. Each step can use a pre defined number of tools. An Agent has autonomy on what and when to use tools and when to stop running. These are the main difference between an agent and a workflow (generally speaking). 

Most people who are building agents are building workflows. Most companies saying they want agents actually just want workflows - and that’s okay!

Agents are hard to get right in production. They’re a lot more autonomous and the room for error is far greater. The amount of testing and guard railing needed for getting agents into production isn’t worth it for most companies. 

Just build AI workflows and reap the rewards. 

DM me if you want to learn how.
